sections.h2: Where is Salem, and how is the city laid out?
sections.html:
Salem is Oregon's capital and the seat of Marion County, in the north-central Willamette Valley. The city covers about 49.6 square miles. The Willamette River runs north through the city and forms the boundary between Marion and Polk counties, so West Salem is in Polk County while the rest of the city is mostly in Marion.

That county line matters to a seller. A house in West Salem and one east of the river can have different county offices, tax collectors and recording steps even though both carry a Salem address.

The 2020 census counted 175,535 residents, which makes Salem the second most populous city in Oregon. Hills frame the city: Salem Hills to the south, Eola Hills to the west at about 1,000 feet, and Waldo Hills to the east at about 600 feet. Elevation inside the city limits ranges from roughly 120 to 800 feet, so some lots are flat valley floor and others sit on slopes.

Salem has 17 recognized neighborhood associations, which are independent groups supported administratively by the city.

sections.h2: What is the history of Salem as a state capital?
sections.html:
Salem grew from the Jason Lee Methodist mission of 1840 and became the territorial capital in 1851 and the state capital when Oregon joined the Union in 1859. The Kalapuya people lived in the area first and called it Chim-i-ki-ti.

The Oregon Institute, forerunner of Willamette University, was set up in 1842, and the town site was established in 1844. The city incorporated in 1857, and the Oregon State Fair was placed here permanently in 1861.

The state capitol burned twice. The first state house was lost in December 1855, and the second capitol, completed in 1876, burned on April 25, 1935. The current building was finished in 1938. Salem's nickname is the Cherry City, from its past cherry-growing industry.

sections.h2: Who are the largest employers in Salem?
sections.html:
State government is Salem's dominant employer, with about 23,500 state employees, which is 26.69 percent of the jobs counted in the city's 2024 financial report. The other large employers are health care, schools, local government and logistics.

Salem is also a food-processing center, with Kettle Foods employing about 700 locally and Oregon Fruit Products canning here since 1935. The Oregon Department of Corrections is headquartered in the city. Median household income was $72,827 in the 2023 American Community Survey.

Public-sector and health-care payrolls make up much of that list, so the local job base looks different from a port or tech-driven city.

sections.h2: What is the weather in Salem, and does it flood?
sections.html:
Salem has a Mediterranean climate with wet winters and dry summers, and yes, parts of the city have a documented flood history. Average annual precipitation is 40.08 inches, most of it from October through April, and July and August together bring only about 2 percent.

The record high is 117 degrees and the record low is minus 12. Flooding is a bigger sales issue than heat.

  • 1861: the largest Willamette flood on record
  • 1964: the Christmas flood crested nearly ten feet above flood stage, caused $157 million in damage and killed 20 Oregonians, and Salem Memorial Hospital evacuated 121 patients
  • February 1996: near 100-year flood levels, and Salem accounted for nearly one-third of Marion County's National Flood Insurance Program claims that year
  • January 2012: more than nine inches of rain in five days in south Salem, flooding in the Battle Creek, Mill Creek, Pringle Creek and Croisan Creek basins, about 300 evacuated and 64 streets closed

The city can tell you whether a parcel is in the FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area or the floodway, and it keeps a flood insurance rate map and an interactive floodplain map. Development Services answers questions at 503-584-4646. If your house sits near a creek, ask for that determination before you set a closing date. See the city's flood history page.

sections.h2: How do people get around Salem?
sections.html:
Interstate 5 runs through Salem, with Oregon Routes 99E, 22, 221, 51 and 213 also serving the city. Route 22 crosses the river into West Salem on the Marion Street and Center Street bridges.

Cherriots runs the local bus network, including regional service to Wilsonville, and Amtrak stops at the Salem station on the Coast Starlight and Amtrak Cascades routes. McNary Field has limited commercial service, and Avelo Airlines started flights to Burbank and Las Vegas in October 2023.

Salem's main drinking water comes from the North Santiam River watershed rather than the Willamette. Other streams in town include Mill Creek, Mill Race, Pringle Creek and Shelton Ditch, and Riverfront Park links to Minto-Brown Island Park by the Peter Courtney bridge, finished in 2018.

The Salem-Keizer School District, with about 39,000 students, is the second largest in Oregon. A small part of Salem in Marion County falls in Cascade School District 5. Willamette University, Corban University and Chemeketa Community College are all in the area, and Willamette is the oldest university in the American West.

sections.h2: When are Marion County property taxes due on a Salem house?
sections.html:
Marion County property taxes are due November 15, February 15 and May 15, and a full payment by November 15 earns a 3 percent discount. Paying two-thirds by that date earns 2 percent on the amount paid, and paying one-third earns none.

Payments postmarked after the due date lose the discounts and are charged interest. When the 15th falls on a weekend or holiday, the due date moves to the next business day. For West Salem in Polk County, check with the Polk County tax office instead.

  • By mail: Marion County Tax Collection, PO Box 3416, Portland, OR 97208-3416
  • Online or phone: Paystation, as listed on the county's payment page
  • In person: Courthouse Square, 555 Court Street NE, with after-hours drop boxes
  • Phone: 503-588-5215

Oregon caps growth in assessed value at about 3 percent a year under Measure 50, so a house owned since the 1990s often has an assessed value far below market. The county payment page has the details.

sections.h2: What must a Salem seller disclose?
sections.html:
Oregon sellers deliver a property disclosure statement to each buyer who makes a written offer, and the buyer has five days after delivery to revoke. The form asks about title, water, sewage, structure, systems, seismic issues and general conditions.

Under ORS 105.470, a sale by a court-appointed personal representative, trustee, conservator or guardian, or by a financial institution after foreclosure, can use a shortened Section 1 form.

Floodplain status, creek drainage and any past water damage are the questions most worth answering carefully on a Salem house.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Salem house with water damage?
faqs.a: Yes. You disclose what you know on the Oregon seller's form, and a cash buyer prices the house as it stands. Floodplain status can be checked with the city's Development Services office.
